newsitem.title: UK: Price, tight oilseeds help up grain use in feed.
newsitem.headline: Price, tight oilseeds help up grain use in feed.

text.p: Cheaper grains, a tight world oilseeds market and changing patterns of animal husbandry have all contributed to an increase in the amount of grain used in animal feed.

The shift was highlighted on Monday by news that the French cereals office ONIC is to announce an 11 percent increase in the amount of grain used in manufactured animal feed, along with a report the same day from the FAO predicting a world wide jump in feed use of cereals.

Under the 1992 reform of Europe's Common Agricultural Policy, prices for grains have come lower, if not by as much as some expected, Steve Thornhill, the director of market information at the Home Grown Cereals Authority said.
Combined with a rise in prices of some substitutes, because of a tight world oilseeds market, this gives a persuasive price incentive to shift.
There has also been a change in livestock production, partly inspired by the fallout from the BSE scare.

Poultry production is expanding faster than other livestock sectors, and it takes more grain in feed. A shift in consumption from beef to poultry, as well as to pork, automatically pushes up the overall proportion of grain used in feed.
More and more of the EU's traditional imported feed ingredients are being used in their countries of origin for feed, rather than being exported, the HGCA's Thornhill said.
He cited manioc and rice bran as two products which are increasingly being used in their countries of origin, rather than exported.
Despite high prices, demand for soyameal is still holding up well, because of bans, inspired by the BSE crisis, on the use of meat and bonemeal in animal feed, Thornhill said.
The fundamental question on the likely future trend in grain use in feed is the extent to which it is a result of the relative price of cereals and non cereal feed ingredients, Thornhill said.
If it is the major element, the relative position of the alternatives might stabilise, as oilseed availability increases.
"It looks as though we're on for a bigger oilseeds crop," he said, citing the soya to maize price ratio in the US as favouring soya, as well as likely increased oilseed rape output in Canada.
